title: Wait for the promise (Acts 1:1–11)
hook: Luke's second volume begins: you will receive power and be my witnesses
tomorrow: twelve became eleven. how do you choose who fills the empty place?

segments.voice: Matthew is read through, ending on a mountain: I am with you, to the end of the age. Today a new book opens, and it starts by pointing back to a former one.
screen: `TO THE END OF THE AGE.` → `A NEW BOOK: ACTS.`

segments.voice: Every group project has someone who starts before the instructions are finished. Acts opens with a goodbye and the opposite instruction. The risen Jesus is with his friends in Jerusalem, and his last orders aren't go. They're stay. Don't leave the city, "but wait for the promise of the Father." Why wait? Because what's coming isn't something they can make themselves: "ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you."
screen: `THE ONE WHO STARTS EARLY.` → `HIS LAST ORDERS: STAY.` → `YE SHALL RECEIVE POWER.`

segments.voice: Before the goodbye they ask the question everyone asks: "Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?" When? Jesus won't give a date: "It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power." He gives a map instead: "ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth." Then "he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight." Christians call it the Ascension. And here the chapter pulls two ways, and Christians have leaned on both. Some hear the first order loudest: wait. Their best case: Acts doesn't begin with a plan, it begins with a pause, and the power that comes isn't the friends' own. Rush, and you're only witnessing to your own energy. Others hear the two men in white loudest: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven?" Their best case: waiting can harden into staring, and the promise was always aimed at the uttermost part of the earth. Stay too long, and nothing reaches anyone. Acts keeps both lines on one page, in order: wait first, then witness. And a witness, in this book, isn't a salesman. A witness tells what they've seen.
screen: `NOT FOR YOU TO KNOW THE TIMES.` · `A MAP: JERUSALEM TO THE EARTH'S END.` · `WAIT: THE POWER ISN'T YOURS.` · `WHY STAND YE GAZING?` · then, large: `YOU SHALL BE WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring up one thing you're itching to do today: a reply, a decision, a purchase. Don't do it, and don't argue yourself out of it. Just wait beside it for these two minutes, the way the friends waited in the city, and notice whether it looks any different at the end.
Wait for the promise. Jesus' last instruction in Acts: stay, and wait for what the Father promised, before you go.
Pocket this one: you shall be witnesses, after the waiting, not instead of it. Acts, page one.

howItsDone: Some churches keep the feast of the Ascension in the Easter season and read Acts 1 that day; some keep the days after it as a time of waiting and prayer before Pentecost.

fork.setup: two friends from church argue at lunch. one says, "pray first, act later." the other says, "enough praying, start doing." which side does Acts 1 take?
options: both, in order: wait for the promise, then go and witness.
only waiting: Jesus' last words were to stay put.
only going: the angels told them to stop praying.
fork.reveal: Acts 1 keeps both lines: 'wait for the promise of the Father' and 'why stand ye gazing up into heaven?' the waiting comes first, and it's aimed at the witness.

chat.meaning: In Acts 1 they wait for the promise before they witness, and the angels' question keeps the waiting from turning into staring. Wait, then go.

Holy Ghost.meaning: older English for the Holy Spirit

Samaria.meaning: the region between Judaea and Galilee

Ascension.meaning: Jesus taken up into heaven, as Christians remember it
